paragraphs: By midday, the rain had thinned to a mist.

Andrew spent the next hour at the north watch post, which was a generous name for a reinforced platform above the outer fence. The view was mostly fields, a narrow road, and the remains of an industrial building whose roof had collapsed long before their unit arrived. Farther out, the earth had been raised into defensive banks with concrete emplacements at intervals.

Yelena Sokolova was already there, leaning against the rail with a cup of tea. Her long braid was tucked inside her jacket against the wind. A battered paperback rested facedown on the ammunition locker beside her.
She glanced at Andrew. “You're early.”
“I'm on time.”
“Then the clock's wrong.”
“I'm deeply reassured by your confidence in me.”
“Someone has to keep your expectations reasonable.”

Andrew took the binoculars from their case. The road below was empty except for a flatbed truck heading west. Its load was hidden beneath a canvas cover, and the driver slowed as he passed the outpost to wave toward the tower.
Andrew raised a hand. The truck continued toward the interior settlements.

For a moment Andrew listened to its engine grow fainter. It wasn't much, but traffic still moved on some roads. People still carried materials, repaired their homes, quarreled over prices, and made deliveries that didn't involve weapons. On the base, it was easy to spend an entire day talking about machines and the next defensive line.
“Any movement?” he asked.
“Two patrol vehicles at the western junction,” Yelena said. “Three birds that nearly caused a diplomatic incident with the motion sensor. One truck with a suspiciously enthusiastic driver.”
“Sounds serious.”
“He waved twice.”
“Definitely suspicious.”
Yelena picked up her book, holding a finger between its pages to keep her place. Andrew noticed the cover: two people in very clean clothes standing in front of a lake.
“Good?” he asked.
“Terrible,” she answered.
“Then why are you on page two hundred?”
“To see if it gets worse.”
Andrew looked at the title. “It has a sequel.”
“Don't tell me things like that.”
He gave her the binoculars and opened the watch log. Yelena had recorded the vehicles, the weather, and a brief description of an animal near the fence.
“Small, four-legged, judgmental,” Andrew read.
“A cat,” Yelena said.
“Why didn't you write cat?”
“I wasn't sure it was ours.”
“Are cats normally assigned to us?”
“They should be. At least a cat would catch something around the ration store.”

They traded reports for a while. Yelena pointed out the swollen drainage channel that ran alongside the eastern road. Andrew could see why Mara had insisted on changing the patrol route. Brown water had spilled into the low ground, and the bridge approach was scarcely distinguishable from the field.
He used the tower radio to call Mara.
“You were right about the crossing,” he said when she answered.
There was a pause. “Say that again.”
“I said the eastern approach is underwater.”
“Not that part.”
Yelena reached over and pressed the transmit button. “Mara, he said you were right.”
“Thank you, Yelena,” Mara replied. “I'll note the time.”
Andrew took his hand off the radio.
“I work with children,” he said.
“You are younger than my favorite pair of boots,” Yelena answered.
“You're eighteen.”
“The boots are very old.”

On the way down, Andrew passed the outpost's little garden. Darius had built two raised beds against the kitchen wall using discarded transport crates. The plants were protected from the wind with clear plastic panels, and most were growing much more stubbornly than their surroundings suggested they should.
Darius was outside, holding a watering can in one hand and examining a row of herbs.
“Is there anything alive in there?” Andrew asked.
“Of course.”
“Anything edible?”
“That's a much more complicated question.”
Andrew looked at the tiny leaves. “How long until dinner?”
“Depends. What are you willing to eat?”
“Not the experimental porridge.”
Darius gave him an injured look. “It was one mistake.”
“And an ambitious one.”
Darius set down the can and brushed soil from his hands. “Dinner's going to be stew. I found beans, potatoes, and enough onions to pretend we planned ahead.”
“Excellent. What do you need?”
“For you to keep Nico away from the ingredients.”
“Unrealistic. Next request?”
“A clean pot.”
Andrew regarded him. “Surely that's the easy part.”
Darius turned toward the kitchen. “You'd think so.”
The afternoon test began just after two.

Juno brought his XR-17 out of the hangar at walking speed, moving across the concrete yard with the careful, uneven rhythm of a machine relearning how to use its legs. Each foot lifted, shifted, and settled with a dull mechanical thud. Heat shimmered behind the reactor housing. The cannon turret remained locked forward, and the missile bays were secured for maintenance.

Andrew stood beside Mara at a painted line a safe distance from the test area. Sera held a diagnostic tablet, its cable now connected to a short-range receiver. Nico wore hearing protection and carried the inspection clipboard as though he'd been promoted for the occasion.
Juno's voice came over their handheld radio.
“Left front leg responding. Load transfer normal. Ready for the turn.”
Mara checked the marked turning area. “Take the slow arc first. No clever tricks.”
“I'm wounded you even think that needs saying.”
“Nico suggested you climb the fuel shed to test clearance,” Mara replied.
From behind the clipboard, Nico said, “That was a theoretical suggestion.”
“It was a terrible theory,” Andrew said.
The XR-17 turned.

Its six feet worked in sequence, front and rear legs adjusting while the center pair carried the load. Andrew watched the left-front joint, where the old bearing had fought every step the day before. This time the foot came around smoothly.
“Temperature?” he asked Sera.
“Steady. More importantly, it's the actual temperature, not the sensor inventing a disaster.”
The machine completed the turn and came to a halt.
“Again,” Mara said over the radio. “Other direction.”
Juno obeyed. The second turn was slower but clean. They checked the data, then made him repeat the cycle with a slightly heavier load before agreeing to let him return to the bay.

When Juno climbed down, sweat had flattened his golden hair against his forehead. He came toward them grinning, with the satisfaction of someone who'd been proved right and intended to be gracious about it.
“She's perfect,” he said.
“She passed a walking test,” Mara corrected.
“Her walking is perfect.”
“Write that on the sheet,” Andrew told him. “Then do the cold check tonight.”
Juno's grin faltered. “You really enjoy paperwork.”
“I enjoy not having to explain why a leg came off.”
“It wouldn't have come off.”
Sera turned the tablet toward him. “That's what I said this morning. Nobody appreciated it.”
Nico ticked the last box on the inspection sheet. His handwriting crowded the margin, but every required test was there.
Andrew checked the page and handed it back. “Good work, all three of you.”
Nico brightened immediately. Juno tried not to look pleased and failed.
Akari appeared from behind the maintenance barrier, camera already in her hands.
“Wonderful,” she said. “The rain stopped. Everybody stay where you are.”
Mara looked at her boots. “We're covered in mud.”
“Authenticity.”
“I'm holding a diagnostic cable,” Sera said.
“Character.”
Andrew pointed toward the hangar. “You said four o'clock.”
“I'm doing practice shots.”
“You have been doing practice shots since breakfast.”
“Then imagine how good the real one will be.”
A drop of water landed on the camera's strap. Another hit Andrew's sleeve. Akari lifted her head as the fine mist became proper rain again.
She closed her eyes.
Nico looked toward the sky. “Maybe four o'clock.”
Akari lowered the camera carefully inside her jacket. “Nobody make plans after four.”
Andrew began to protest, remembered he'd already lost this argument, and let her have it.
